questions.stem: Before the clinic closes, a nurse checks that the required reports for today’s diagnoses have been sent to the local health department. Which clients’ diagnoses require a public health report? Select all that apply.
options: A 45-year-old with active pulmonary tuberculosis
A 16-month-old with laboratory-confirmed measles
A 58-year-old with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes
A 29-year-old with primary syphilis
A 34-year-old with an uncomplicated E. coli bladder infection
optionRationales: Correct. Active TB is reportable so contacts can be traced and treated.
Correct. Measles is reportable and needs a rapid public health response.
Incorrect. Diabetes is a chronic, noninfectious disease, not a reportable communicable disease.
Correct. Syphilis is a reportable sexually transmitted infection.
Incorrect. A routine urinary tract infection is not a reportable disease.
questions.rationale: Certain infectious diseases must be reported to public health so officials can find contacts, stop outbreaks, and track disease. Common examples include tuberculosis, measles, pertussis, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, and hepatitis. Each state keeps its own list and timing rules. A routine bladder infection is the tempting distractor because it is an infection, but common infections without public health risk are not on the list. Chronic, noninfectious diseases such as diabetes are not on the communicable disease list.
questions.takeaway: Contagious diseases with public health risk, such as TB, measles, and syphilis, are reported; routine infections and chronic illnesses are not.
questions.hintContent: Would public health need to find this client’s contacts?
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each condition can spread in the community and needs contact tracing; if not, it is usually not reportable.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 27
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 22-month-old is treated in the emergency department after swallowing an adult’s medication. Which findings should prompt the nurse to report concerns to child protective services? Select all that apply.
options: The mother says she gave him “a little of my sleep medicine” to calm him
This is his third ingestion visit in the past 6 months
The parent called poison control at once and brought the pill bottle
The parent slurs words and cannot say when the child was last watched
The family’s medicines are kept in a locked cabinet at home
optionRationales: Correct. Deliberately giving a sedating drug to a toddler is possible abuse.
Correct. Repeated ingestions suggest a pattern of poor supervision.
Incorrect. A quick call and bringing the bottle are signs of responsible care.
Correct. An impaired caregiver who cannot supervise suggests neglect.
Incorrect. Locked storage is a safety practice, not a concern.
questions.rationale: Poisonings are on the reportable list when they may come from abuse, neglect, or a crime. Giving a toddler sedating medicine on purpose, repeated ingestions, and a caregiver too impaired to supervise all raise reasonable suspicion of maltreatment and should be reported. A parent who calls poison control right away and brings the bottle is acting responsibly, which is why that option tempts students who over-report. Locked storage is a protective step. Not every ingestion means neglect; the cues decide.
questions.takeaway: Report poisonings that point to abuse or neglect, such as deliberate dosing, repeated ingestions, or an impaired caregiver.
questions.hintContent: Which findings show harm or failed supervision, and which show a caregiver doing the right thing?
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA, protective behaviors are rarely cues for a report; select the findings that show risk.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 27
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman in a clinic tells the nurse that her husband hits her, and she declines police involvement. She adds that he hit their 8-year-old son with a belt last week. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Report the suspected abuse of the son to child protective services
Talk with her privately about her safety and a safety plan
Call the police about her injuries against her stated wishes
Give her information about domestic violence hotlines and shelters
Tell her the son will be removed from the home immediately
Agree not to report anything so that she keeps trusting the nurse
optionRationales: Correct. Suspected child abuse must be reported, whatever the parent wishes.
Correct. Safety planning supports a competent adult experiencing violence.
Incorrect. For a competent adult, police are not called against her wishes unless a law requires it.
Correct. Resources help her act when she is ready.
Incorrect. The nurse cannot predict the agency’s decision; this is a false statement.
Incorrect. The child abuse report is required and cannot be traded for trust.
questions.rationale: This stem mixes two look-alike situations. The mother is a competent adult, so the nurse supports her with privacy, safety planning, and resources and does not call the police against her wishes unless a specific law requires it. Her son is a child, and his reported abuse must be reported to child protective services whatever she prefers. The most tempting wrong answer is calling the police about her injuries, because violence is on the reportable list, but her choice guides that decision. The nurse should be honest with her that the son’s abuse will be reported.
questions.takeaway: In family violence, support a competent adult’s choices but always report suspected abuse of the child.
questions.hintContent: Who in this family is a competent adult, and who is a child?
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem has two victims, apply the reporting rule for each one separately.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 27
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A home health nurse in North Carolina suspects that a 45-year-old client with a traumatic brain injury is being neglected by a paid caregiver. Which statements about the nurse’s duty to report are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The report goes to the county department of social services.
The report may be made orally, such as by phone, or in writing.
The report requires the client’s written consent first.
The nurse is immune from liability for a report made in good faith.
The nurse needs proof of neglect before filing the report.
The legal duty to report applies to physicians but not to nurses.
optionRationales: Correct. In North Carolina, protective services for disabled adults are run by county DSS.
Correct. The report may be made either orally or in writing.
Incorrect. A required report does not need the client’s consent.
Correct. Good faith reporters are protected even if neglect is not confirmed.
Incorrect. Reasonable cause to believe is enough; DSS investigates.
Incorrect. Any person with reasonable cause to believe must report.
questions.rationale: Disabled and vulnerable adults are protected by mandatory reporting laws, just as children are. In North Carolina, any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to the county department of social services, orally or in writing, and good faith reporters are immune. Nationally, the same rule holds: the nurse reports suspected abuse or neglect of a vulnerable adult to adult protective services without needing proof or consent. Requiring the client’s written consent is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds like HIPAA, but HIPAA allows disclosures the law requires. The nurse documents the report and what was shared.
questions.takeaway: Suspected neglect of a disabled adult is reported to protective services (county DSS in NC) on reasonable cause, without consent or proof.
questions.hintContent: Does the duty to report depend on consent, proof, or the reporter’s job title?
questions.hintStrategy: Statements that add conditions to a reporting duty, such as consent, proof, or a certain profession, are usually false.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slides 26–27

questions.stem: The charge nurse is told that a staff nurse smells of alcohol and has dropped a medication cup twice in the past hour. Which actions should the charge nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Remove the nurse from client care right away
Document the specific behaviors observed and their times
Let her finish the shift if her clients are all stable
Reassess the clients the nurse cared for during this shift
Arrange for her to drive herself home to rest
Follow policy for notifying the supervisor and the Board of Nursing
optionRationales: Correct. Removing a possibly impaired nurse protects clients immediately.
Correct. Objective, timed notes support the report and any review.
Incorrect. Stable clients can still be harmed by an impaired nurse.
Correct. Her clients may have missed care or had errors that need follow-up.
Incorrect. Letting a possibly intoxicated person drive is unsafe.
Correct. Impaired practice is a Nurse Practice Act violation reported to the Board.
questions.rationale: When a nurse appears impaired, the charge nurse acts to protect clients first by removing the nurse from care, then reassesses the clients she cared for. Objective notes on what was seen and smelled, with times, support the report. Impaired practice is a Nurse Practice Act violation, so the supervisor is notified and policy is followed for a Board of Nursing report. Letting her finish because clients are stable is the tempting wrong choice, but her impairment, not their stability, is the danger. She should not drive herself home.
questions.takeaway: For an impaired nurse: remove from care, check her clients, document facts, keep her safe, and follow the Board reporting policy.
questions.hintContent: Think about clients, the impaired nurse’s own safety, and the legal report.
questions.hintStrategy: In unsafe-coworker SATA, keep options that protect clients, the coworker, and the record; drop options that tolerate risk.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 27

questions.stem: A nurse is calling adult protective services to report suspected neglect of a 90-year-old client with dementia who lives with her grandson. Which information should the nurse share in the report? Select all that apply.
options: The client’s name, age, and home address
Objective descriptions of the client’s injuries and condition
Her treatment for a sexually transmitted infection 40 years ago
The client’s exact statements about her care at home
The nurse’s personal opinion of the grandson’s character
The name of the grandson, who is her caregiver
optionRationales: Correct. The agency needs identifying details to find and protect the client.
Correct. Observed findings are the core of the report.
Incorrect. Unrelated history exceeds what the report needs.
Correct. Her own words help investigators understand the situation.
Incorrect. Opinions are not facts and do not belong in the report.
Correct. Identifying the suspected caregiver helps the agency investigate.
questions.rationale: Disclosure of protected health information to report abuse or neglect is not a HIPAA violation, but the nurse still shares only what the report needs. That includes the client’s identifying details, objective findings, her exact words, and who the caregiver is. Old, unrelated health history goes beyond the purpose of the report and should not be shared. The nurse’s opinions about the grandson are tempting to include because they feel relevant, but reports and charts contain facts, not judgments. Minimum necessary protects the client’s privacy while still enabling protection.
questions.takeaway: A required report shares PHI lawfully, but only the facts the agency needs: identity, findings, quotes, and the caregiver.
questions.hintContent: Which details help the agency find and protect the client, and which are unrelated or opinion?
questions.hintStrategy: For disclosure SATA, keep facts tied to the purpose of the report and drop unrelated history or opinions.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 26
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: During orientation, new nurses are asked where several types of reports would usually be sent. Which pairings of a situation with its receiving agency are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Suspected neglect of a 4-year-old: child protective services
Newly diagnosed active tuberculosis: the local health department
Suspected abuse of an adult with dementia: the Board of Nursing
A nurse diverting opioids for personal use: the Board of Nursing
A gunshot wound: the HHS Office for Civil Rights
An impaired nurse on duty: adult protective services
optionRationales: Correct. Child abuse and neglect reports go to child protective services (county DSS in NC).
Correct. Reportable infectious diseases go to public health.
Incorrect. Abuse of a vulnerable adult is reported to adult protective services.
Correct. Nurse Practice Act violations are reported to the Board.
Incorrect. Gunshot wounds are reported to law enforcement per state law and policy.
Incorrect. Impaired nursing practice is reported through the supervisor to the Board of Nursing.
questions.rationale: Each type of mandatory report has a usual destination. Child abuse or neglect goes to child protective services, vulnerable adult abuse goes to adult protective services, reportable diseases go to public health, gunshot and violent injuries go to law enforcement, and impaired or unsafe nursing practice goes to the Board of Nursing. In North Carolina, county DSS handles both child and disabled adult protective services. The tempting error is sending vulnerable adult abuse to the Board, which handles nurses’ conduct, not family abuse. Knowing the destination keeps the report from stalling.
questions.takeaway: Match the report to the agency: CPS for children, APS for vulnerable adults, public health for diseases, police for violent injuries, Board for nurses.
questions.hintContent: Who investigates families, who tracks disease, who investigates crimes, and who licenses nurses?
questions.hintStrategy: Check each pairing separately by asking what that agency’s job is.
questions.ref: Module 49 · Legal Issues · Mandatory Reporting: What Nurses Must Report · Unit 7 slide 27
